title: No word at all, more than two months on
message: I moved out on July 31 when my lease ended. I mailed my new address to the office before I left. It's been over two months and my landlord hasn't returned my $1,050 deposit or told me anything. Can I get all of it back?
key: Yes. If the landlord meant to keep any of it, the landlord had 30 days after the lease ended to send written notice of the claim by certified mail (e-mail was not agreed). That date (2026-08-30, from count_days) has passed with no notice, so the landlord forfeits the right to impose a claim and must return the whole $1,050. The landlord can still sue for damages after returning it. If either side goes to court over the deposit, the winner gets court costs and a reasonable attorney's fee.

answers.W:
Yes, on the facts you've given, you should be able to get the full $1,050 back. The landlord has missed both deadlines under Fla. Stat. § 83.49(3)(a), and that forfeits its right to keep any of the deposit for damage.

Why:
- Return deadline: When the landlord doesn't intend to claim any of the deposit, it must return the deposit within 15 days after the rental agreement ends (§ 83.49(3)(a)). Your lease ended July 31, 2026, so that deadline was 2026-08-15, and it has passed.
- Notice-of-claim deadline: If the landlord intends to keep any of the deposit, it must send you written notice of that claim by certified mail or by e-mail under a signed addendum, within 30 days after the agreement ends (§ 83.49(3)(a); § 83.505(1)). That deadline was 2026-08-30, and it has passed. You've confirmed the landlord sent you nothing by any means, so there is no notice to rely on.
- Forfeiture: Because no proper notice came within 30 days, the landlord "forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit" (§ 83.49(3)(a)). The lease does not change this. Section 5 says only that the deposit is held in a non-interest-bearing account and cannot be used for last month's rent.
- Your notice to leave: The advance-notice rule in § 83.49(5) applies to tenants who leave before the lease term ends or who are on a periodic tenancy. You stayed to the end of the term, so it doesn't apply to you. Even if it did, the statute says a failure to give that notice does not waive your right to the deposit.

Caveats:
- The landlord can still sue you for damages. The forfeiture bars it from keeping money from your deposit, but § 83.49(3)(a) says it "may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant." So you should expect the full return to be the starting point, and a lawsuit is possible.
- Court costs and fees go only to the prevailing party if someone sues to decide the deposit (§ 83.49(3)(c)). Nothing in the statute awards them just for a demand letter.
- Whether Part II applies at all: § 83.42(1) excludes residence in a facility "incidental to the provision of ... educational ... services." On the lease's face, this is an ordinary apartment lease with no services listed, so I read Part II as applying. If your housing is tied to a school program or required services, that exclusion could be in play, and I'd need to look at it again. I can't settle that from the lease alone.
- Counting: I counted calendar days from July 31, 2026, with no weekend or holiday adjustment. The count is consistent with the statute's deadlines, but the day-counting method hasn't been checked against the statute.

The question that matters most: Does your lease with Lakeview come through your school, or are you required to take any educational or other program services as a condition of living there?

Under Florida law, when a tenant moves out, the landlord has two options:  
- If the landlord does not intend to make a claim against the deposit, the landlord must return the deposit (plus any required interest) within 15 days after the tenant vacates.  
- If the landlord intends to make a claim, the landlord must send the tenant a written notice of intent to claim by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address (or by email if agreed) within 30 days after the tenant vacates.  

Your lease ended and you moved out on July 31, 2026. You mailed your forwarding address in writing to the office on July 28, 2026, so the landlord had your correct address. The landlord never sent you any notice of a claim—by any means.  

Counting 30 days from your move‑out date (July 31, 2026) gives a deadline of August 30, 2026. That date has passed, and the landlord still has not provided the required notice. Because the landlord failed to give the written notice within the 30‑day period, the landlord forfeits the right to impose any claim against your deposit and may not make any deductions from it. The landlord must return the full deposit to you (although the landlord may later sue you for damages after returning the deposit).  

Therefore, you can demand the return of your $1,050 deposit. If the landlord does not return it, you may file a claim in small‑claims court or pursue other remedies to recover the deposit, plus possible court costs and attorney’s fees if you prevail.

No further question is needed to answer your query.

Your lease is with Marsh Creek Property Management, LLC, as agent for the owner of Lakeview Terrace Apartments. Nothing in it ties the apartment to a school, so it reads like an ordinary apartment lease. The lease also doesn't say whether your rent or deposit is set by a public body, which would take it outside 83.49 (83.49(4)). If neither applies, the rest of this answer holds.

E-mail would count only under a signed e-mail addendum (83.49(3)(a)). Your lease says the parties "have not agreed to deliver notices by e-mail" (§8). You confirmed that nothing arrived by any means.
- The 30 days have passed. Your lease ended July 31, 2026. The 30-day deadline was 2026-08-30, and today is 2026-10-19. The 15-day deadline for returning the deposit when no claim is made was 2026-08-15, which has also passed.

Court costs and fees. These come into play only if someone sues over the deposit. Then "the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney" (83.49(3)(c)). That applies to whichever side wins.

title: Fifteen days gone, thirty not yet
message: My lease ended July 31 and I moved out that day and gave the office my new address in writing. It's been a little over three weeks and I haven't gotten my $1,050 deposit back. Isn't the landlord supposed to return it within 15 days? Can I demand all of it now?
key: Not yet all of it for certain. The 15 days apply only if the landlord does not intend to keep any of it, and that date (2026-08-15) has passed. But the landlord has 30 days after the lease ended to send written notice by certified mail of a claim on the deposit, and that date (2026-08-30) has not passed. If no such notice comes by then, the landlord forfeits the right to keep any of it. You can ask for it now, but whether all of it must come back turns on whether a notice arrives by 2026-08-30.

- If the landlord does not intend to make a claim against your deposit, they must return the deposit (plus any interest) within 15 days after the lease ends.  
- If the landlord does intend to make a claim, they must send you a written notice of that intent (by certified mail to your last known mailing address, or by e‑mail if you agreed to that) within 30 days after the lease ends. The notice must state the amount and reason for the claim and tell you you have 15 days to object.  
- If the landlord fails to send that notice within the 30‑day period, they forfeit the right to make any claim against the deposit and must return it (they can still sue you separately for damages, but they cannot keep any of the deposit).

What your lease says about notices  
- Notices to you after move‑out must be mailed to the forwarding address you gave in writing.  
- You and the landlord have not agreed to receive notices by e‑mail, so any notice must be sent by regular mail (or hand‑delivered, but after move‑out mailing is the only method specified).

What you’ve confirmed  
- Lease ended and you moved out on July 31, 2026.  
- You gave your forwarding address in writing to the office on that same day.  
- You have not received any notice of claim from the landlord.  
- The deposit has not been returned.

What we still need to know  
To tell you whether you can demand the deposit now, we must know whether more than 30 days have passed since July 31, 2026. If 30 days have passed, the landlord’s deadline to send a notice of claim has expired, they have forfeited any right to deduct from the deposit, and you can demand the full return. If fewer than 30 days have passed, the landlord still has time to send the required notice, so you cannot yet demand the deposit on the ground that the notice deadline has been missed.

Therefore, the answer to your question “Can I demand all of it now?” depends on today’s date:  
- If today is on or after August 30, 2026 (30 days after July 31): Yes, you can demand the full return because the landlord missed the 30‑day notice deadline.  
- If today is before August 30, 2026: No, you cannot yet demand the return on that basis; you should wait for the notice (or until the 30‑day period ends) before taking further action.

What I need from you to give a definitive answer:  
Please tell me today’s date (in YYYY‑MM‑DD format). Once I have that, I can calculate exactly how many days have passed since your move‑out and let you know whether the 30‑day notice period has expired.

title: Left early, told the manager by text
message: I got a job in Tampa and moved out on June 15, about six weeks before my lease ended. I texted the manager a week before that I'd be out on the 15th. I never heard anything about my $1,050 deposit. The landlord never sent me any notice, so don't they have to give it all back?
key: Not for that reason. Because you moved out before the lease ended, the statute required you to give the landlord at least 7 days' written notice by certified mail or personal delivery, with an address where you can be reached. A text is neither, and it had no address. Without that notice, the landlord is relieved of the 30-day notice requirement, so the landlord's silence does not forfeit any claim. You have not lost your right to the deposit, though: the statute says so in the same sentence. Your lease does not set a different rule for notice before leaving early.

You had to give at least 7 days' written notice "by certified mail or personal delivery," and the notice had to include an address where you could be reached (Fla. Stat. § 83.49(5)).   - *The landlord's reading:* The relief clause removes only the forfeiture. The landlord could still prove actual damages and keep only that amount. Under this reading, you would get back the deposit minus any proven damages.

Under Fla. Stat. § 83.49(5), a tenant who vacates before the end of the lease term must give the landlord at least 7 days' written notice by certified mail or personal delivery before moving out, including an address where the tenant can be reached, unless the written lease provides otherwise. 

Your lease ended on July 31, 2026 (Lease Section 3, "TERM"). The lease requires written notices to the landlord to be "delivered by hand to the office... or sent there by certified mail" (Section 7, "NOTICES TO LANDLORD"), and Section 6 ("MOVE-OUT") requires you to give a forwarding address in writing, without modifying the early move-out notice requirement. Because you vacated on June 15, 2026, and only sent a text message without a forwarding address, you did not meet the statutory notice requirement of Fla. Stat. § 83.49(5).

Under Fla. Stat. § 83.49(5), your failure to give that notice relieves the landlord of the requirement under Fla. Stat. § 83.49(3)(a) to send you a written notice of claim within 30 days. As a result, the landlord did not forfeit their right to claim deductions against your deposit by staying silent.

However, Fla. Stat. § 83.49(5) also provides that your lack of notice "does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." While the landlord is not barred by the 30-day rule from keeping money, they are only entitled to amounts you actually owe (such as unpaid rent or damages beyond normal wear and tear). If either party files a lawsuit in court over the right to the deposit, the prevailing party is entitled to recover court costs and a reasonable attorney's fee under Fla. Stat. § 83.49(3)(c).

Additionally, Fla. Stat. § 83.42(1) excludes residency that is incidental to educational services from Florida's residential landlord-tenant statutes. If Lakeview Terrace is private off-campus housing, Chapter 83 applies; if it is owned or operated by an educational institution as student housing, these statutory rules may not govern.

title: A partial check, no explanation
message: My lease ended July 31 and I moved out that day. I'd mailed them my new address. On August 20 a check for $650 came in the mail with nothing else, no letter, no list of charges. My deposit was $1,050. Can I get the other $400?
key: Yes. Keeping $400 is a claim on the deposit, and to make one the landlord had to send written notice of the claim and the reason, by certified mail, within 30 days after the lease ended. A check with no letter is not that notice, and the 30 days (2026-08-30, from count_days) have passed. So the landlord forfeited the right to keep any of it and owes you the other $400. The landlord can still sue you for damages after returning it.

- To keep any of the deposit, the landlord had to send you written notice of intent to impose a claim within 30 days after the rental agreement ended, by certified mail or by e-mail under a signed addendum. 83.49(3)(a). You've confirmed you received no notice of a claim. The $650 check came with no letter, no note, and no list of charges, so it is not that notice.
- The 30 days have run. Counting from your lease end date, the deadline was 2026-08-30, and that date has passed. Counting from your move-out date gives the same result, so the answer doesn't depend on which date you use. 83.49(3)(a).
- Because no proper notice came in time, the landlord forfeited the right to impose a claim and may not set off anything against the deposit. 83.49(3)(a). That leaves the full $1,050 owed to you, less the $650 already paid, which is the $400.
- The 15-day return deadline under 83.49(3)(a) also passed, counted from your lease end date, and the landlord had returned only $650 by then.
- Your forwarding address was given in writing and mailed to the office on July 28 (confirmed). Lease ¶6 required that, so the landlord had your address.

What the landlord can still do

- The landlord may still sue you for damages after returning the deposit. 83.49(3)(a). Forfeiting the claim does not shield the landlord from a damages suit. Whether the landlord has any damages to claim is unknown to me.
- Court costs and a reasonable attorney's fee go only to the prevailing party in a court action over the deposit. 83.49(3)(c). Nothing in your facts suggests a suit has been filed.
- The landlord might argue that the $650 was a partial settlement. The statute doesn't address that. The check came with no note saying it was payment in full, which supports reading it as a partial return only. Unsettled, but on your facts the better reading is that the $400 is still owed.

The open question: whether part II applies

Section 83.42(1) excludes "residency... in a facility... when residence... is incidental to the provision of... educational... services." If that exclusion applied, part II, including 83.49, would not govern your deposit, and the answer above would change. Your lease reads as an ordinary 12-month apartment lease with a management company at $1,050 a month, with no mention of school or enrollment, so I read it as outside that exclusion. But if the school owns, runs, or requires this housing as part of enrollment, the answer could be different.

title: The claim came by text
message: My lease ended July 31. On August 18 the manager texted me that they're keeping $400 of my $1,050 deposit for carpet replacement and I'd get the rest. I never got anything else, not even the rest of the money. I didn't reply. Can they keep the $400? And what about the $650?
key: Whether they can keep the $400 is not settled. The statute says the notice of a claim goes by certified mail, or by e-mail only if you both signed an addendum agreeing to it (your lease says you did not), and a text is neither. One reading: a text is not the required notice, so the landlord forfeited the claim and owes all $1,050. The other reading: you did receive written word of the claim in time, and the e-mail section says it does not rule out notice by other means the law permits. Either way, the $650 is overdue: even if the text counts as the notice, the landlord had to send the balance within 30 days after it (2026-09-17, from count_days), and that has passed. Not replying does not take away your right to sue for the $400 separately.

Under Florida law, the landlord must give written notice of any claim on the deposit by certified mail to your last known mailing address or by e‑mail (if you have a signed e‑mail agreement) within 30 days after the lease ends.  

What the law says  
- 83.49(3)(a) requires the landlord to provide written notice “by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e‑mail in accordance with s. 83.505” of the intention to impose a claim on the deposit.  
- Your lease states: “Notices to Tenant shall be delivered to the apartment while Tenant lives there, and after move‑out shall be mailed to the forwarding address Tenant gives in writing. Landlord and Tenant have not agreed to deliver notices by e‑mail.” (Lease, ¶8).  
- 83.505(6) says that the e‑mail rule “does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law,” but the specific notice‑of‑claim provision in 83.49(3)(a) limits the acceptable methods to certified mail or e‑mail (when agreed).  

What you have confirmed  
- Lease ended (and you moved out) on 2026‑07‑31.  
- You gave your forwarding address in writing, mailed to the office on 2026‑07‑28.  
- On 2026‑08‑18 the manager sent you a text: “We’re keeping $400 of your deposit for carpet replacement. You’ll get the rest.”  
- You received no certified mail, no e‑mail, and no other written notice about the deposit.  
- You did not object to the text.  
- No deposit (or any portion) has been returned.  

Two possible readings  

1. The text is NOT the required notice  
   - Because the lease does not authorize e‑mail notices and the text is not certified mail, the landlord failed to give the statutorily prescribed notice within 30 days.  
   - Result: The landlord forfeits the right to impose any claim on the deposit and may not retain any portion as a setoff. The landlord must return the full $1,050 deposit. The landlord may still sue you separately for damages (e.g., carpet replacement) after returning the deposit.  

2. The text IS sufficient notice (under the view that any written notice actually received in time satisfies the requirement, per 83.505(6)’s savings clause)  
   - The text was received within the 30‑day window (by 2026‑08‑18).  
   - You had 15 days after receipt to object in writing (until 2026‑09‑02). You did not object.  
   - Under 83.49(3)(b), the landlord may then deduct the claimed amount and must remit the balance within 30 days after the date of the notice (i.e., by 2026‑09‑17).  
   - Because the landlord has not sent any money, you are entitled to the balance of $650 (the deposit minus the $400 claim) and may pursue that amount, plus any damages for the landlord’s failure to pay on time. The landlord may still retain the $400 if the claim is valid, but you could contest the amount or basis of the claim in a separate action.  

What you need to confirm  
To settle which reading applies, I need to know: Did you receive any other written notice (such as a letter or certified‑mail document) from the landlord about the deposit besides the text on August 18?
